title: What We Forgot About Teaching Reading Comprehension and How Remembering Can Help with LLMs
author: Yu, Terry
summary: Terry Yu traces the history of summarizing instruction from Brown and Day's 1983 macrorules -- which identified the operations of skilled summarizers but answered only the cognition question, not the pedagogy question -- to Palincsar and Brown's 1984 reciprocal teaching study, which showed that comprehension is a discursive practice acquired by being hosted inside structured conversation with an expert who takes the turns the novice cannot yet take, then hands them back. Palincsar's insight was that summarizing is one move among several that constitute comprehension, and pulling it out of that conversational process to drill it in isolation destroys the mechanism by which novices actually acquire it. As reciprocal teaching scaled, it underwent what Brown and Campione called a 'lethal mutation': the teacher's responsive scaffolding was replaced by scripted role-cards and labeled worksheets that preserved the surface features of the 1984 study while destroying the interior mechanism that made it work. The WWC's 'mixed effects' finding on reciprocal teaching is what a lethal mutation looks like in aggregate data: classrooms with teachers doing the real responsive work got results; classrooms with the scripted imitation got nothing; the two averaged to 'mixed.' Yu argues the four moves (question, summarize, clarify, predict) transpose directly to LLM pedagogy -- students develop a genuine working theory of the model's capabilities by being hosted inside a structured conversation about AI output. The active ingredient is the teacher's improvisational responsiveness; any attempt to package the approach into a worksheet or rubric will lethally mutate it for the same systemic reasons that destroyed reciprocal teaching forty years ago.
points: Brown and Day's 1983 macrorules correctly described what skilled summarizers do (delete trivial material, substitute superordinate terms, select or invent topic sentences), but these rules answered only the cognition question -- they could not explain how a struggling student gets from outside the practice to inside it, which is the pedagogical question that matters.

Palincsar's 1984 reciprocal teaching study showed comprehension is an internalized conversation acquired by being hosted inside structured dialogue with an expert who takes the turns the novice cannot yet take, then hands them back -- the teacher's professional judgment is the signal, not the noise, and no script can replace moment-to-moment responsiveness.

The 'lethal mutation' (Brown and Campione, 1996) names the failure mode where an educational innovation is scaled by operationalizing its visible surface features while the interior mechanism is removed: four strategies became four worksheet boxes, responsive scaffolding became a script, assessment moved to product rubrics -- all surface features intact, active ingredient absent.

The four reciprocal teaching moves transpose directly to LLM pedagogy -- question (what do we actually want from the model?), summarize (what did we get and what does it mean?), clarify (where does the output hold and where does it not?), predict (what if we push back?) -- but only if the teacher's responsiveness remains the active ingredient.

Teachers who recognize what Palincsar and Brown were actually doing in 1984 already have everything they need for LLM pedagogy; the teachers waiting for the binder will not get one that works -- the active ingredient cannot be encoded into a script by the same systemic forces that destroyed reciprocal teaching.
quotes: Summarizing is one move among several that together constitute what skilled readers do when they comprehend, and a written or verbal 'summary' is a byproduct of comprehension. Pulling it out of that process, holding it up as the point of reading a passage, and drilling it in isolation was, Palincsar suspected, part of why it would not stick.

The instructional principle Palincsar and Brown articulated was deceptively simple. The teacher relinquishes the task to the novice only at the level the novice can negotiate at this moment. As the novice becomes more competent, the teacher increases her demands -- one stage further into the zone of proximal development.

A lethal mutation is a change that preserves the surface features of the original -- the parts that are visible, namable, and easy to operationalize -- while destroying the interior mechanism that made the original work. The mutated version looks like the thing, but superficially. And because it looks like the thing, the people implementing it cannot tell that they have lost what mattered.

By the end of the three steps, what was happening in classrooms labeled 'reciprocal teaching' had no functional resemblance to what Palincsar and Brown had done in 1984. The surface features were all present. The four strategies were taught and practiced. Students took turns. The teacher modeled and faded. But reciprocal teaching was gone.

The reciprocal teaching being implemented was a fluent execution of the observable features of the 1984 study, conducted in the complete absence of the thing the 1984 study was about. This is what makes the mutation lethal rather than merely incomplete.

An innovation that works has to scale, scaling means going to teachers who were not part of its development, those teachers need materials, materials require specification, specification favors the observable over the interior, the observable features get codified, the codification becomes the program, and the program is what fidelity is measured against.

Notice what this is not. It is not a prompt-engineering curriculum. It is not a set of rules for using AI responsibly. It is not a worksheet with boxes labeled Question, Summarize, Clarify, Predict. The moment it becomes any of those things, it has been lethally mutated, and we are back at the macrorules with a different label on the anchor chart.

The teacher who can do this work is doing the same work Palincsar's teachers were doing with Sara in 1984 -- hosting a novice inside a discourse she is gradually internalizing, increasing the demands one stage further into the zone of proximal development as the novice becomes capable of more.
